props.title: Made in Dagenham
props.initialSlug: Working women fight for equal pay in 1960s UK

sections.content: **Made in Dagenham** (2010) brilliantly captures the pivotal 1968 Ford sewing machinists' strike that helped establish equal pay legislation in the UK. Sally Hawkins delivers a powerhouse performance as Rita O'Grady, following in the tradition of other working-class labor films like Norma Rae (1979) and **Silkwood** (1983). The film excels at showing how local activism can spark national change, similar to how **Pride** (2014) depicted miners' strike solidarity and North Country (2005) tackled sexual harassment in Minnesota's mines.

sections.content: The 1960s-70s labor movement spawned several outstanding films capturing working women's struggles. 9 to 5 (1980) used comedy to address workplace sexism, while **Silkwood** (1983) took a darker approach examining whistleblower Karen Silkwood's suspicious death. These films share DNA with **Made in Dagenham**'s mix of personal drama and systemic critique, showing how individual courage catalyzes collective action.

Director Nigel Cole brings the same warmth and humor to **Made in Dagenham** that he brought to Calendar Girls (2003), another story of ordinary British women achieving extraordinary things. The film's attention to period detail - from the fashion to the factory floor - rivals **The Hour** (2011) and **An Education** (2009) in capturing 1960s Britain's social upheaval. sections.content: **Made in Dagenham** joins a proud tradition of British working-class cinema including **Brassed Off** (1996), **The Full Monty** (1997), and **Billy Elliot** (2000). These films share a knack for finding humor and humanity amid serious social commentary, using personal stories to illuminate broader struggles for dignity and fairness.
